name: Sunderland
title: Thickness Measurement in Sunderland | Coasters and Bulk Ships
description: Ultrasonic thickness measurement in Sunderland for coasters, short-sea bulk and general cargo ships: hold, hatch cover and ballast tank gauging alongside.
h1: Ship Thickness Gauging at the Port of Sunderland on the River Wear
intro: Sunderland, where the River Wear meets the North Sea, was once among the world's great shipbuilding towns; its last yard closed in 1988. The Port of Sunderland, owned and run by the city council, now receives coasters and short-sea cargo ships carrying bulk and general cargo, steel and project shipments. Most calls are short discharges, so gauging is fitted around cargo work hold by hold. Technicians fly from India to Sunderland for each ship, since Atlantis keeps no one stationed in north-east England.
keywords: general cargo ship inspection north east

highlights.p: Coasters and small bulk and general cargo ships come into the Wear, discharge and sail again within a short stay. Hatch covers, coamings and weather deck can be gauged while cargo comes out, and each hold as soon as it is empty and swept.

highlights.h: A shipbuilding river without a yard
highlights.p: The Wear's building berths and repair docks have gone, so ships that need docking book a yard on the Tees or the Tyne. Sunderland is where the readings for that docking can be taken alongside, before the yard slot is confirmed and the steel ordered.

highlights.h: Older ships near heavy renewal surveys
highlights.p: Much of the European coaster fleet is well into its second or third decade, which puts these ships into the renewal surveys that call for the most gauging. An owner's condition survey during a Sunderland call shows how much renewal the next survey is likely to demand.

port.h: Sunderland and the Wear: a council-run port at the river mouth
p: The Port of Sunderland occupies the mouth of the River Wear, on the North Sea coast between the Tyne and the Tees. Two piers protect the entrance, Roker Pier on the north side with its lighthouse and the New South Pier opposite, and behind them the port has quays along the lower river and enclosed docks on the south side, including Hudson Dock and Hendon Dock. Unlike most English ports of its size, it is owned and operated by the local authority, Sunderland City Council, which has been redeveloping the riverside land around it. The port is compact: a ship entering the harbour is alongside within minutes, and the berths are close together, which suits an inspection team moving between holds, deck and tanks with its equipment.

For more than a century the Wear was a shipbuilding river. Yards such as Doxford and Austin & Pickersgill turned out tramp ships, tankers and cargo liners, and Austin & Pickersgill's SD14, a standard cargo ship design, was built in large numbers and traded worldwide for decades. The last yards closed in 1988, and the river's working life now depends on the port. Today's traffic is mainly short-sea: coasters and small bulk and general cargo ships carrying bulk and breakbulk cargo, steel, and occasional project shipments on heavy-lift or multipurpose ships. These ships trade between the north-east of England, the near Continent, Scandinavia and the Baltic, and most of them make many calls a year at ports of this kind.

The entrance faces the North Sea and takes the brunt of north-easterly weather, so in winter a ship's arrival can slip by a tide or a day when the swell at the harbour mouth is heavy. Once inside the piers, ships lie in sheltered water and the weather has little effect on work alongside. Calls are usually short and driven by the cargo: a coaster may discharge in a day or less and sail on the next suitable tide. Some ships wait at the port for a cargo or for orders, and those quieter stays are the best chance to open ballast tanks and double-bottom spaces that a busy discharge leaves closed. Gauging plans here therefore come in two sizes, a focused scope for the discharge and a fuller one for a ship that is staying.

facilities.h: Quays and docks for gauging at Sunderland
p: At the river quays, the gauging plan follows the discharge. Hatch covers and coamings are measured from the deck while cargo operations continue, holds are taken one at a time as the stevedores finish them, and the team works out of the way of grabs and crane hooks. Hold frames, brackets, lower hopper plating and tank tops are where cargo damage and wastage show first on a coaster, so those come first in each hold. Ballast tanks are only entered if the crew has prepared them in advance and the master has issued an entry permit, which is why we ask the superintendent to have the tanks pumped and ventilated before arrival.

In the enclosed docks, ships waiting for cargo or orders give a calmer window, and tanks can be opened in turn over a longer stay. There is no working drydock on the Wear that we would plan around. A ship trading to Sunderland that needs docking goes to UK Docks' four-dock yard on the Tees or to the drydocks at Hebburn on the Tyne, and readings taken alongside in Sunderland beforehand let the yard plan its steel renewal before the ship arrives.
list: River quays: hold, hatch-coaming and deck gauging on coasters during discharge, one hold at a time.
Hudson Dock and Hendon Dock: ships waiting for cargo or orders, where ballast tanks and double bottoms can be opened over a longer stay.
Heavy-lift and project cargo calls: crane pedestal weld checks and tank-top gauging beneath heavy units.
UK Docks on the Tees and the Hebburn drydocks on the Tyne: where a ship trading to Sunderland goes for docking after an afloat survey here.

context.h: Inspection drivers for short-sea ships on the Wear
p: The Maritime and Coastguard Agency carries out port state control in Sunderland, as a member of the Paris MoU. The Paris MoU targets ships by risk profile, weighing ship type, age, flag and company performance and the ship's own inspection history, and older general cargo ships tend to fall into the higher-risk groups that are inspected more often and in more depth. Corroded hatch covers, wasted air pipes and leaking weather-deck structure are the kind of finding that leads to a detention. Owners who know where their ship's steel stands, from a recent gauging, deal with those findings before an inspector raises them.

Most coasters calling at Sunderland are below 5,000 gross tonnage, which keeps them outside the EU Emissions Trading System and FuelEU Maritime even when they trade to European ports. For these ships the pressure to gauge comes from class surveys and from the market rather than emissions rules. Dry-cargo charterers increasingly screen ships through RightShip or their own vetting, and buyers in the busy second-hand coaster market want to see steel condition before they commit. A thickness record taken during a cargo call answers both without taking the ship out of service.

jobs.h: Typical gauging work on the Wear
jobs.p: Sunderland jobs are small-ship jobs. The holds and tanks are compact, so a two-person team can achieve a lot in a single discharge if the ship is prepared. Most requests come from owners and managers of short-sea fleets who want a condition check before a renewal survey, a docking or a sale, and who would rather do it during a commercial call than send the ship somewhere specially. We plan each one around the cargo programme the agent gives us, and agree in advance which holds and tanks matter most.

Owner's condition survey on a twenty-year-old general cargo ship ahead of its fourth renewal survey.

Ballast tank and double-bottom gauging on a ship waiting at a dock berth for its next cargo.

logistics: Newcastle International Airport is the usual arrival point, and the Tyne and Wear Metro runs from the airport through to Sunderland, which makes the last part of the journey straightforward. Technicians travel from India on UK visit visas, applied for well before the ship's expected call. Port access is controlled by the port's ISPS arrangements, with passes requested through the ship's agent, and the agent's berthing schedule tells us when holds will be free.

faqs.q: Can holds be gauged while cargo is still being discharged at Sunderland?
faqs.a: Yes, one hold at a time. The team works in a hold once the stevedores have finished it and the grab or crane has moved on, starting with frames, brackets, hopper plating and tank top where wastage and cargo damage concentrate. Hatch covers and coamings are measured from the deck in parallel. If the discharge finishes quickly, priorities agreed with the superintendent decide which holds are covered.

faqs.q: Where does a ship trading to Sunderland go for a drydock?
faqs.a: The Wear no longer has a working repair yard, so ships book a dock on the Tees, where UK Docks has four drydocks, or on the Tyne at Hebburn, or at a yard across the North Sea. Gauging alongside in Sunderland before the docking gives the yard a steel list in advance, which helps the superintendent agree the repair specification and avoid surprises once the ship is dry.

faqs.q: Does North Sea weather affect gauging work at Sunderland?
faqs.a: Inside the piers, hardly at all; the berths are sheltered and work alongside carries on in most conditions. The effect is on arrival. Heavy north-easterly swell at the harbour entrance can delay a ship by a tide or more in winter, so we keep the team's dates flexible and confirm the berthing time with the agent before the technicians travel to the port.

faqs.q: Is a condition survey worth doing on an older coaster before a sale or new charter?
faqs.a: For ships in their second or third decade, usually yes. A focused survey of holds, hatch covers, ballast tanks and the double bottom shows the buyer or charterer where the steel stands, and shows the seller what a buyer's surveyor is likely to find. Done during a cargo call, it costs the ship no extra port time and gives both sides a common set of readings.
